title: National Grid Reference Map: Plot Any Reference
description: Plot any Ordnance Survey grid reference on the National Grid Reference Map — see its square, its context and the point it names. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, type a six-figure reference from a walking guide and watch its 100-metre square land on the map — the moment a string of letters and digits becomes a place you can see.
quick_answer: The National Grid Reference Map plots an Ordnance Survey grid reference on the map, with its square and surrounding grid context drawn in. Type a reference and watch it land, or click the map and read its reference — the visual bridge between paper maps and geography.
steps_intro: A reference is an address. See where it lives:

body.t: Walking guides and site reports cite references blind. Plot one before the walk and the car park, gate or summit it names is confirmed — convert coordinates the other way with the
A reference on a form becomes a visible square: does it sit on the building, the field or the neighbour's garden? The map answers faster than any description.
The 1 km and 10 km grid context around a plotted reference shows students how squares nest — the abstraction becomes landscape.
Finds logged by reference get plotted for the site meeting — a table of strings becomes a distribution map.

examples.label: Example · The square is the statement

body.t: A six-figure reference names a 100 m square, and the map draws that square — not a pin pretending to metre precision. What the reference claims is exactly what you see.
A transposed digit usually lands the square in a lake, a motorway or the wrong county — the map's context is a lie detector that pure conversion cannot be.

popular_table.note: The drawn square is the reference's whole claim — the point lies somewhere inside it. Longer references shrink the square; they never move its truth beyond the source's accuracy.

faq: Why does the map draw a square instead of a pin?
Because a grid reference names an area, not a point — the square is the honest picture of what the reference says.
Can I plot several references at once?
Plot them one at a time to inspect each; lists of references belong in GIS, with this map as the visual spot-check.
What if my reference has spaces?
Spaces between the letters and digit groups are cosmetic — 'TQ 292 796' and 'TQ292796' name the same square.
The square landed in the sea.
Either the reference is wrong (a transposed digit is the usual cause) or it genuinely names a coastal square — the context view makes the call obvious.
Does the map show OS mapping itself?
The map plots references on standard web map data with grid context; Ordnance Survey's own copyrighted mapping is viewed through OS channels.
How do I read a reference off the map?
Click the ground — the map returns the reference for the clicked point at your chosen precision, the reverse of plotting.
